# Generated by bench/stages.py from models/web_service/model.yaml.
# The finished model with everything the book has not introduced by the end
# of ch08 removed, so that a reader can see it at 49 nodes. Not a model
# anybody would ship. Do not edit: say which chapter introduces a node in
# build-order.yaml instead.
dsl: 1
model: web_service_regime
title: >-
  A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts — The
  working set outgrows memory
currency: USD
description: The web service model as it stands at the end of ch08.
nodes:
  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 3000.0
        likely: 8000.0
        maximum: 20000.0
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — the busy hour, not the daily mean. Triangular,
        because this is an engineer's lowest, most likely and
        highest values; claiming more precision would be invention.
    range: [500, 40000]
  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how
      much you hold today. Nobody can count next quarter's busy
      hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they
      grow, and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the
      level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The service owners estimate what the service holds today:
        its database and the objects users have uploaded, before
        replication, indexes or compression. It has not been counted
        yet, and counting it would turn the estimate into a fact.
    range: [1, 200]
  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    distribution:
      lognormal:
        p10: 1.12
        p90: 1.6
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and the factor
        cannot be zero or less. One future in ten grows by less
        than 12% a year, and one in ten by more than 60%; outside
        that range you would be surprised. One factor for requests
        and for records, because users drive both.
    range: [1.0, 2.0]
  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: the refresh cycle this fleet is bought against
    range: [3, 8]
  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n
      the n is a pure number, so the horizon has to be divided
      by something with the same units before it can be used as
      one. Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year
  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
  cores_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core/host
    value: 16
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        spec sheet: physical cores. A hyperthread is not a core,
        and a sheet that counts threads doubles this number without
        doubling the work a host does
    range: [4, 128]
  ram_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 64
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        spec sheet: the modules fitted. The sheet says 64 GB and
        means GiB — appendix D — and the operating system will
        report less than either, which is os_reserve's job
    range: [8, 1024]
  os_reserve:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 0.06
        likely: 0.1
        maximum: 0.18
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        the share of memory the kernel, the agents and the page
        cache floor keep before the service sees any. Triangular:
        a floor, a usual figure, and a host with too many agents
        on it
    range: [0.0, 0.4]
  ram_for_service:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per host
    note: >-
      Gibibytes in, decimal terabytes out — the build converts
      (appendix D). Declared in the unit the working set is counted
      in, so that the chain which divides one by the other rounds
      a count of hosts and not a count of hosts times nine hundred
      and thirty-one.
    formula: ram_per_host * (1 - os_reserve)
  peak_to_mean:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: peak-to-mean ratio
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 2.0
        likely: 3.5
        maximum: 6.0
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — the busy hour against the daily mean. Triangular,
        and it is a property of your traffic that belongs to the
        estate target: nothing here can measure it
    range: [1.0, 10.0]
  mean_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: mean request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate / peak_to_mean
  service_demand:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: second * core / request
    label: CPU time per request
    note: >-
      Core-seconds of work one request costs, which is not how
      long a request takes. A request that occupies one core for
      twelve milliseconds has a service demand of twelve milliseconds
      whether it returns in twelve milliseconds or in twelve seconds
      — the difference is queueing, and Part II is about that
      difference.

      This is the model's one rate constant and it belongs on
      a rig (ch03). No rig is declared, so it is held here as
      an assumption whose source says what would replace it, rather
      than as a measured node with nothing behind it.
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 0.008
        likely: 0.012
        maximum: 0.02
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The lowest, likeliest and highest values are this book's
        own choice for the running example: not measured on any
        machine, not taken from any product. It is held as an
        assumption because no reference machine is declared in
        `rig/machine.yml`; `make measure-rig` on a declared machine
        replaces it with a measured one. It is triangular, with
        three values, because it has not been measured. Once it
        is, it becomes a normal spread around the measurement,
        which is a change of claim and not only of numbers (ch13).
    range: [0.002, 0.05]
  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: host
    value: 54
    label: hosts in the fleet
    note: >-
      **The most important node in this model, and the one a spreadsheet
      hides.** Sizing does not produce a fleet; it produces a
      recommendation, and then a person decides. It arrives here,
      in Part II, because a queue needs something to stand in
      front of — but it is decided in ch12, and everything downstream
      of it, every dollar, every watt, every ceiling, is a consequence
      of the number chosen here and not of the number the model
      would recommend in hindsight.

      Suppose the fleet were worked out afresh in each future,
      from that future's own inputs; it would sit inside every
      margin it was sized against, in every future. The ceilings
      that check those margins would then report no chance of
      crossing them, which is true by definition but tells you
      nothing. Holding the fleet as an input, one number the team
      decided, lets the ceilings ask: given what was bought, how
      often do the futures cross the line?
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The sizing decision, taken the usual way: the host count
        the model recommends (from ch10), worked out with every
        input at its point estimate. Change this number and watch
        the ceilings move; that is ch12's exercise.
    range: [4, 200]
  one_host:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: host
    value: 1
    note: >-
      as elsewhere: a conversion has to be a host before the division
      means anything
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  one_core:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: core
    value: 1
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  one_request:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: request
    value: 1
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores in the fleet
    formula: hosts * cores_per_host
  busy_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores busy at the busy hour
    note: >-
      Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of cores
      doing work, it has nothing to do with how many you own,
      and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_demand
  utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: busy_cores / cores
  service_seconds:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: service time
    note: >-
      service demand with the core divided out: how long one request
      would take alone
    formula: service_demand * one_request / one_core
  in_flight_unqueued:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in flight, if none waited
    note: >-
      Little's law with the residence time equal to the service
      time: the fewest requests that can be in the system at this
      arrival rate. ch06 uses the residence time instead, which
      adds the time a request waits, and this number goes up.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_seconds
  utilisation_cap:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation the model will admit to
    note: >-
      A modelling choice, stated rather than hidden. The waiting-time
      formula below divides by what is left of the fleet, so at
      a utilisation of one it divides by zero and returns infinity.
      Infinity is not a prediction. Past this point the formula
      has stopped describing a queue and started describing an
      arithmetic accident, so the model clamps and the ceiling
      reports that it is over.
    value: 0.98
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: where this model stops being about queues (ch06)
  queueing_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.3
    label: queueing margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch06 — the share of the fleet kept idle at the busy hour.
        The ceiling lets utilisation go up to one minus this margin,
        and no further. Declared once, it is used by the ceiling
        that checks utilisation at the busy hour (ch06), the ceiling
        on utilisation counting coordination (ch07), the chain
        that sizes the fleet for requests (from ch10) and the
        ceiling with one host lost (ch11), so they cannot drift
        apart.
    range: [0.0, 0.6]
  effective_utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: min(utilisation, utilisation_cap)
  residence_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: residence time
    note: >-
      Service time divided by the share of the fleet that is idle.
      That is the formula for one server with one queue, applied
      here to the whole fleet; a fleet of many cores sharing one
      stream of requests waits less than this at the same utilisation
      (ch06).
    formula: service_seconds / (1 - effective_utilisation)
  waiting_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: time spent queueing
    formula: residence_time - service_seconds
  concurrency:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in the system
    note: >-
      Little's law: the number of requests in a system is the
      rate they arrive at times how long each one stays. It assumes
      no pattern of arrivals and no order in which requests are
      served. It holds while the system is in a steady state:
      as many requests leaving as arriving. ch05 is about what
      that buys and what it does not.
    formula: peak_request_rate * residence_time
  queueing_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation at the busy hour
    of: utilisation
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      Not a capacity limit: a fleet that is busy most of the time,
      but short of fully busy, has not run out of anything; it
      has a queue in front of it. The margin is large because
      crossing it is paid for in waiting time by every request,
      not in a failure that pages the people on call (ch06).
  host_count:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: hosts / one_host
  single_host_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second/host
    label: throughput of one host alone
    note: >-
      Every core of a host busy on requests and nothing else:
      the cores divided by the CPU time each request costs. The
      straight line of ch07 is this times the host count, and
      it is the line nobody has ever measured.
    formula: cores_per_host / service_demand
  contention:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: contention
    note: >-
      The fraction of the work that cannot be done in parallel:
      a lock, a single writer, a shared queue. It costs a fixed
      share of every host you add, so it flattens the scaling
      curve and never bends it downwards.
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 0.002
        likely: 0.005
        maximum: 0.015
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch07 — an assumption: it has not been fitted for this
        service; a fit from throughput measured at three fleet
        sizes, one a single host, would replace it. Triangular,
        because a fit gives a central value and a range rather
        than a shape. Its maximum is the end to distrust: a serial
        fraction can always be worse than the one you measured.
    range: [0.0, 0.05]
  crosstalk:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: crosstalk
    note: >-
      The cost of hosts having to agree with each other, which
      grows with the number of pairs rather than the number of
      hosts. This is the term that makes the curve turn over:
      past some count, the next host costs more in agreement than
      it brings in work.
    distribution:
      lognormal:
        p10: 1.5e-05
        p90: 9.0e-05
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch07 — an assumption, not fitted for this service, though
        the same measurement as contention's would replace it:
        a fit from throughput at three fleet sizes, one a single
        host. It is the harder of the two to fit because it shows
        only in how the curve bends at larger fleets, and the
        three measured sizes usually sit at the small end. Lognormal,
        because it is wide and cannot be negative, and because
        a shape should not assert a hard upper limit on a quantity
        this weakly known.
    range: [5.0e-06, 0.0003]
  linear_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: throughput if scaling were free
    formula: hosts * single_host_throughput
  achievable_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: achievable throughput
    note: >-
      The universal scalability law. One host's throughput times
      the host count, divided by what contention and crosstalk
      take back. With crosstalk at zero, it approaches Amdahl's
      limit and never falls; with both at zero, it is `linear_throughput`:
      the straight line.
    formula: linear_throughput / (1 + contention * (host_count - 1) + crosstalk * host_count * (host_count - 1))
  scaling_efficiency:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: achievable_throughput / linear_throughput
  scaling_loss:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the fleet doing nothing useful
    of: 1 - scaling_efficiency
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.5
    because: >-
      At the margin, half the fleet's work is lost: one host in
      two does no useful work. The loss is to contention and to
      coordination between hosts. Nothing fails and nothing pages
      anyone; the fleet costs twice what its work is worth. A
      budget is the only thing this ceiling protects (ch07).
  peak_hosts:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: where adding hosts stops helping
    note: >-
      Where the scalability curve turns over, from the two coefficients
      alone: the square root of one-minus-contention over crosstalk.
      Past it, throughput falls. It is a property of the software,
      not of the budget, and no amount of money moves it.
    formula: one_host * sqrt((1 - contention) / crosstalk)
  headroom_to_peak:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the peak already built
    formula: host_count / (peak_hosts / one_host)
  utilisation_including_coordination:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    note: >-
      The same fleet's utilisation, worked out from what it can
      deliver rather than from what its hosts could deliver alone.
      It is higher than `utilisation` whenever the fleet has more
      than one host, and equal at one host. The gap is the work
      the hosts do on each other's behalf.
    formula: peak_request_rate / achievable_throughput
  optimism:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: how much the queueing view understated it
    formula: utilisation_including_coordination / utilisation
  coordination_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    of: utilisation_including_coordination
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      This ceiling keeps the queueing margin, the same margin
      as the ceiling labelled utilisation at the busy hour. It
      applies the margin to the capacity the fleet can deliver,
      counting coordination, rather than to the capacity its hosts
      would have alone. Where the two ceilings disagree, this
      one is about the system you own (ch07).
  hot_fraction:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of records touched in a busy hour
    distribution:
      triangular:
        minimum: 0.01
        likely: 0.03
        maximum: 0.08
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch08 — the working set as a share of everything held.
        Triangular; nobody measures this and everybody has an
        opinion, and the maximum is a service whose users all
        look at the same week's data
    range: [0.005, 0.3]
  working_set:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: working set at horizon
    formula: stored_data * hot_fraction
  cache_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: cache margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch08 — how much of the fleet's memory is kept free of
        the working set, for its own daily swing and for the process
        heaps. Declared once, the ceiling on the working set checks
        against it (ch08), and from ch10 so does the chain that
        sizes the fleet for memory, so the two cannot drift apart.
    range: [0.0, 0.6]
  fleet_ram:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: memory the service can use, whole fleet
    formula: hosts * ram_for_service
  cache_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: working set against memory
    of: working_set / fleet_ram
    limit: 1
    headroom: cache_margin
    because: >-
      Past the limit, memory cannot hold the whole working set,
      so some reads go to disk. A request's time then includes
      waiting for those reads, and the model has no term for that
      wait, so the service time per request is no longer the number
      this model was built on. Nothing in a chain of multiplications
      says what it becomes (ch08), and the margin is the working
      set's own daily swing.
outputs:
  - mean_request_rate
  - utilisation
  - in_flight_unqueued
  - residence_time
  - waiting_time
  - concurrency
  - queueing_headroom
  - achievable_throughput
  - scaling_efficiency
  - optimism
  - peak_hosts
  - headroom_to_peak
  - scaling_loss
  - coordination_headroom
  - working_set
  - fleet_ram
  - cache_fill
correlations:
  - a: peak_request_rate_t0
    b: service_demand
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      The unhappy one. A busier service is usually a slower one
      per request — caches miss more, locks are held longer, the
      garbage collector runs while somebody is waiting. Treating
      the two as independent understates the tail of every figure
      in this model, and it understates it exactly when the fleet
      is busiest.
